utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good afternoon. The next witness should be brought in, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir. Welcome to the Tribunal. Would you please read allowed the affirmation on the card which is shown to you now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Please sit down. I hope you will receive Dutch interpretation. Is that the case?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Thayer has some questions for you, I suppose. Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good afternoon to you and Your Honours. Good afternoon to the Defence. Good afternoon, everyone in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Would you please state and spell your name, for the record.

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS
utterances.text: I am Vincentius Egbers, E-g-b-e-r-s.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And, sir, do you recall testifying in this courtroom over a period of three days in October of 2006?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And did you recently review all of your testimony in that case, the Popovic case?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS
utterances.text: That's also correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And when we met some weeks ago, were two errors noted at that time? And I'll go over them in a moment.

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: If we look at page 2715 of the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And we don't need to call it up on e-court. It's pretty minor -- minor typos.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: At line 25, there is a reference to the shelling of your position at Bravo 1 wherein, at line 25, it states that: "One of my privates was injured." And, in fact, two UN personnel at that location were injured; is that correct? And you wanted to correct that?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS
utterances.text: That is correct. That is indeed what I wanted to correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And very quickly if we go to 2882 of the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: We don't need to put it up on e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: There is a reference at page -- I beg your pardon, at line 14 referring to the VRS shelling of the column of civilians fleeing from Srebrenica town to Potocari. There is a reference to 40 metres from the colony, and you wanted to change that to 40 metres from the column; is that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, do you also recall reviewing your Popovic testimony in connection with your name being listed as a potential Prosecution witness in the ongoing case against Radovan Karadzic? Do you remember doing that in 2009?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And in that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Could the Court Usher assist the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I think the witness is -- just try not to electrocute yourself.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for your kind words.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Thayer, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: In connection with that review, and for the benefit of the Defence, I am looking at the witness statement of the witness dated 4 September, 2009. This isn't part of the package before this Trial Chamber but for the benefit of the Defence. During of course of your review of the Popovic testimony in 2009, you noted that your answer at page 2863, line 1 should have been: "That is not correct." You told the investigators at that time that, and I quote: "I did see armed Muslim men flaunting the fact that they had new weapons, but this was in July 1995 after the fall of the enclaves, I stated at page 2862, line 18, and not in May 1995." Do you recall telling the investigators that, sir, and do you stand by that correction?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS
utterances.text: Yes. I agree with the correction.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And just for -- to be a little even more complete, you further added, and I quote: "When I answered 'that's correct,' on page 2863, line 1, I was still thinking of July 1995 since I had just previously been discussing seeing Muslim men with weapons during the fall of the enclave in July 1995." Do you recall saying that to the investigators as well?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer. Please look at line 19 of page 3 -- no, sorry, line 21, of page 3, there is a reference to the Popovic testimony in 2009.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. That reference to 2009 -- and I'll just clarify this with the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: 2009 is when you met with the members of the Karadzic Prosecution team and reviewed your Popovic testimony from 2006; is that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS
utterances.text: Are you asking me or the Judge?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I am asking you, sir. Do you recall that it was in 2009 when you met with the members of the Karadzic Prosecution team and reviewed your Popovic testimony from 2006?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, bearing in mind, sir, those three corrections that we've noted for the record, can you attest that the testimony that you read accurately reflects what you said during the trial in the Popovic case?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And can you attest that were you asked the same questions today that you were asked back in October of 2006 in the Popovic trial that your answers would be the same?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, the Prosecution would tender P1142, the transcript of the witness's testimony in the Popovic case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And I have a number of exhibits to tender. The Prosecution would tender P1144 to P1166, recognising, obviously, that we will deal with P1143, the NIOD statement, and P1167, which is the Dutch version of the witness's OTP statement during his examination-in-chief, since those two items were not part of the 92 bis package originally.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer, the exhibits P1163 through P1166 and 67 were not used -- were used but not admitted in the Popovic trial. Are you going to use them today or tomorrow with this witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I will use P1164, P1165, and P1166. Upon an additional review are the unmarked maps which were then marked in the Popovic trial by the witness. So they are simply two maps which you have a marked-up version of, so although it will leave two P numbers hanging out there, I think we will not -- we will withdraw our motion to tender those two exhibits, and I do intend to show the witness P1167. P1163 I had intended to ask the witness a couple of questions about, but then took it off my list to save some time, but now you remind me that it's one of the documents that were not actually admitted in the Popovic case. So I think it is important enough for the Trial Chamber to have before it, so I will ask a couple of questions on that document, unless the Trial Chamber is willing to accept it based on its use in the Popovic trial. Again, it's one of these documents that was shown to the witness, he was questioned on it. I think it's important, therefore, for the Court to have the full context so you can see the document even without me asking additional questions. Absent that ruling, decision, then I will use it today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. The Chamber will receive the documents P1144 through P1162. As you know, the procedure this Chamber is following would need an additional showing the relevance of the other exhibits we were talking about. You may tender them at the best point in time.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Before I read the 92 bis/92 ter summary for Mr. Egbers, I do have a couple of corrections to note which are independent of the witness's testimony, and I don't think there is any dispute about this. I haven't had a chance to let the Defence know, but they are simply corrections that -- two mistakes that were made to some exhibit numbers in the transcript. The first is at transcript page 2917, one of the Defence counsel referred to Prosecution Exhibit P02045, that's a video. However, that is the wrong cite. There is no such video. The correct number should be P02047. I just wanted to note that for the record so there is no confusion when the Trial Chamber is reviewing the witness's testimony is looking for a P number that is incorrect. Similarly, at transcript page 2925, Defence counsel calls out Exhibit D225 and the proper number should be Exhibit 2D00025. And, again, at transcript page 2928, Defence counsel calls out for Exhibit D224, and the correct exhibit number is 2D00024. I think the exhibits will make a little bit more sense when you are matching up our exhibit list and the Registry's exhibit list with the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. This is helpful.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And I think my witness summary will take a couple of minutes. Again, this witness testified concerning a number of matters which are central to the forcible transfer case. The witness served in the Royal Dutch Army from 1988 to 1998. In July 1995, he was a first lieutenant serving as a platoon commander in DutchBat's Charlie Company, located in Potocari. By July of 1995, owing to VRS restrictions on leave, his platoon was reduced from 30 to 20 men. DutchBat could not carry out its mission owing to VRS restrictions on fuel, ammunition, food, and leave. On 8 July, the witness was ordered to take up a blocking position to the west of Srebrenica town, near the road leading from Srebrenica to OP Alpha. He commanded four APCs that remained at this location, near the area of Bajramovici and referred to as Bravo 1 for four days, from the evening of 8 July until 11 July. From his position, he saw a VRS tank fire on Srebrenica and his position, as well as VRS soldiers with dogs entering homes in Pusmulici village and burning them. He did not see the 9 July order from Major Franken to prevent with all available means a breakthrough by the VRS into the town. While he was at Bravo 1 on 9 and 10 July, the VRS fired directly on his position. When his position was first shelled by the VRS, he was not sure if he was the target because there was a Muslim artillery piece nearby, an M-48, though it was never fired. He, the witness, and two of his men were injured by the VRS shelling and the APC was damaged. When he moved to another position nearby, the VRS shelled him again. This was direct shelling of his position which followed him as he drove away from the position, so close air support was ordered. After the close air support on 11 July, the VRS tank which had been firing at his position was no longer firing, so he returned to the Bravo Company compound in Srebrenica, where hundreds of civilians had gathered. He accompanied the fleeing Muslims north to Potocari, carrying wounded and mentally ill on his APC. On the way to Potocari, they were shelled on the left and the right by the VRS. On 12 July, the witness escorted the first convoy to Kladanj, which had Major Boering toward the front, although they did not know where the convoy was headed. En route, people in Bratunac screamed and threw things at the buses. Along the road, Serb soldiers were deployed every 20 metres facing south, some firing. There was an anti-aircraft gun on a vehicle near Sandici. Near Nova Kasaba, he saw between 100 and 200 men kneeling on a football field, lined up with their hands on their necks and guarded by the VRS. He also saw a table and men walking on the road with their hands on their neck walking towards the football field. On 13 July, in the morning, he saw men being separated from their families in Potocari; the men were taken to the white house and the women were pushed inside the buses. He then heard a woman screaming. When he asked her what was happening, she told him that her man had been taken to the white house. He entered the house which was guarded by VRS soldiers who told him that the men would be taken to Kladanj. The men's belongings were in front of the house. The men were terrified, and when they asked him what would happen to them, the witness repeated what the VRS soldiers had told him, namely, that they would be taken to Kladanj. However, the Muslims did not believe that and told him that they would be killed. They included elderly men and younger boys. The witness saw a convoy with the men and boys leave escorted by peacekeepers; however, he was told that the VRS forced the peacekeepers out of their vehicle at gunpoint near Bratunac. Later in the morning of 13 July, he escorted another convoy to Kladanj. En route, Bosnian Serb soldiers took his helmet and vest at gunpoint. There were hundreds of Bosnian Serb soldiers along the road. When he passed the football field near Nova Kasaba again that morning, he saw a few hundred Muslim men there. On the way back from Kladanj, Bosnian Serb soldiers stopped his car at gunpoint and took it. He joined about a dozen other peacekeepers who had also been escorting convoys and who had been stopped by Bosnian Serb forces at Nova Kasaba and had their vehicles taken. When he asked to see the commander of the local Bosnian Serb forces to complain about the Serb forces stopping the peacekeepers, taking their equipment, and threatening them, he was introduced to Major Zoran Malinic, who told him that he was in charge of the headquarters there and of the soldiers who had stopped the witness. Malinic was headquartered in a nearby school building and had an office with his name on the door. Malinic's office had maps of the enclave marked with the UN OPs. With the help of a Bosnian Serb soldier who translated, the witness compiled a written complaint of the Bosnian Serb soldiers' conduct towards the peacekeepers, including stealing UN vehicles and equipment, and forcing a Dutch peacekeeper to ride on top of a stolen APC driven by a Serb soldier and tell the Muslims in the woods it was safe to come out. Malinic told the witness that he did not have anything to do with the troops who were along the road all the way the Bratunac and that he had to contact his commanding officer, Colonel Beara, who was the person who could get the peacekeepers returned to Potocari safely. Nearby the school, there was a small structure in which 20 to 30 [Realtime transcript read in error "230"] men and boys were detained, one of whom had a black eye and one of whom had a stomach wound. The next morning, Colonel Beara arrived in a luxury civilian car. Beara was a tall man with grey hair and the atmosphere of a colonel. The witness remembered him as a big, giant colonel. The witness and Beara saluted each other and were introduced to each other by the Serb interpreter. The witness gave Beara a written copy of his complaint about the conduct of the Bosnian Serb forces. The witness also complained to Beara about Serb soldiers pretending to be UN peacekeepers --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer, I think you should slow down a bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I will. The witness also complained to Beara about Serb soldiers pretending to be UN peacekeepers by wearing stolen UN clothes and driving stolen UN vehicles. Beara took the complaint and entered the school with Malinic. After about an hour -- I beg your pardon, after about half an hour, Beara left. The witness identified Beara from a video he was shown. Later that evening, after there were no buses left to be escorted to Kladanj, the witness and the other peacekeepers were taken back to Potocari. When the witness returned to Potocari he typed up a report the detailing, among other things, his experience at Nova Kasaba and contacts with Malinic and Beara which he submitted the next day, 15 July 1995. Now, I recognise that was a lengthy summary, Mr. President, but I think it will help place in context some of the questions I have for the witness, as well as, I expect, a certain amount of the cross-examination and potential redirect, although I hope some of the redirect may be cut off by some of the questioning I have now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Thayer. If you look at line 18 of became 10, you will find the number at the end of this line. Could you please clarify if this is the correct, to have "20 to 230."

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, for catching that. That's "20 to 30."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, I have a few questions for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: No, I think it's again recorded in a different way, it should read "20 to 30" and not "230"; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I think we have got it now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, when you left the Royal Dutch Army in 1998, what rank did you hold?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS
utterances.text: At the time, I was a first lieutenant. And in 1998, I transferred to the airforce.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And would you please provide the Trial Chamber with just a brief overview of your employment from the time you entered the airforce to the present, including what rank you currently hold?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS
utterances.text: In 2000, I started working as a captain for the Royal Dutch Military constabulary, that's the military police for the armed forces. I am now a colonel for the same Royal Dutch Military constabulary.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, if we may have P1163.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Colonel, I would like to ask you a couple of questions about this document. Please the Trial Chamber just briefly what is this document that we are looking at?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS
utterances.text: This is a questionnaire drafted in English that was presented to me in 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And do you recall how soon after your departure from the enclave was this questionnaire given to you to complete?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS
utterances.text: I don't remember the exact date anymore. Isn't it at the bottom?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I am afraid it isn't, sir, but let me ask you this: If we look at the first page, just to give us a range of possible dates, there is a question here, it says: "It may be necessary for staff of the international tribunal to conduct a further interview ... please indicate any date when you would be unavailable." You indicate here 10 to 18 August of 1995. Is it thus fair to say that whenever you filled this out it was sometime between the time you left the enclave and the 10th of August, 1995?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS
utterances.text: Of course, we completed this immediately after arriving in Zagreb, but I am not sure what the exact date was.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. And just to be clear, Zagreb was your first stop after leaving the Srebrenica enclave; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, if we go to the second page in this document, and I think you testified to some degree about this topic in Popovic, but I think it could bear a little bit of clarification or repetition here. There is the question: "How many persons carried out the capture?" And you indicated on the first page that your freedom of movement had been restricted, and here you write: "We were not captured. We were free to go, but the BSA couldn't guarantee our safety. We tried to drive back with three UN Mercedes. After 500 metres, two of them were stolen." Now, in Popovic, and I just note at transcript page 2760, you testified quite plainly that you were not free to go, and you said the same thing in the Krstic case. So my question to you is: Can you explain your answer here on this form, on this questionnaire, and what you meant when you testified in Popovic and in Krstic that you were not free to go?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS
utterances.text: When I was at the school in Nova Kasaba, I was not handcuffed, my hands were free, but that didn't mean that I could leave. Guns were pointed at me, but I wasn't locked up. That's why my description was somewhat awkward in this respect when I returned to the enclave. We couldn't leave, but we weren't trapped in a prison or cage as the Bosnian men were kept.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Your Honour, at this time the Prosecution would tender P1163.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received as P1163.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And if we may have P1164, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, sir, what we are looking at here on the left in English is an English translation of a document which you filled out by hand in Dutch. The --

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I note two things for the record, Mr. President. First is that the actual -- unfortunately, the actual Dutch official version which was referred to in the Popovic case, for some reason, was not part of the 92 bis package. The translation -- the English translation and the B/C/S translation obviously are, and they are in e-court, but the original Dutch version was not part of the 92 bis package. But we have uploaded it and the Prosecution would tender it as it is obviously the core document for the English translations which were part of the 92 bis package. I'd just discovered that problem this afternoon, and I think we've managed to get the Dutch version uploaded into e-court. Is it possible to display the Dutch version? If not, I can put it on the ELMO. We can just look at it very quickly. And then we will go back to the respective English and B/C/S translations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Just a moment. We have a problem with our screens. We don't have the transcript at the moment. I think we need a technician to assist us.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I think the time changes caught everything off-guard. Okay. I have got a hard copy. We can put the Dutch version on the ELMO very quickly, please, with the assistance of the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We don't have the transcript in e-court at the moment. I was told the same happened to the other courtrooms. We can only follow the transcript on LiveNote, which brings up another problem. We can't see the ELMO and the transcript at the same time, but we should use the time as best as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I will be very brief, Mr. President, with this document. And what I can do is, once the witness has talked about a couple of the pages, I can circulate that hard copy to the -- to the Chamber, and if the Defence doesn't have a copy it can be passed on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We have now the document on the ELMO on our screens. Is everybody able to see that document on the ELMO? Mr. Tolimir, do you have this document on the ELMO in front of you? Okay. I take it that you can continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Colonel, can you identify what this document is on the ELMO for us, please?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS
utterances.text: This is once again a debriefing form, a report that I completed.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. And if you would kindly just remove that first page and we will look at the second page very quickly. In English there is, in the middle of the page, a paragraph which states the following: "This is the end of the first operational de-brief." Do you recall who was conducting this debrief? Was it the UN, was it the Dutch government? Do you have any recollection?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS
utterances.text: This was Dutch.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And if we could just move the page up a little bit, so we could catch the bottom, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Can you just read what number 2 there says into the record, and we'll look at the translation shortly, but if you could just read what number 2 in your handwriting says.

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS
utterances.text: "Regarding our safety, filed a complaint with Major Zoran (see report head S2/3), escorted convoys as assigned, BSA unable to guarantee our safety."

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And if we could remove that next page and look at the next document.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Can you tell the Trial Chamber what this document is, sir, please?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS
utterances.text: This is the document I drafted in the enclave on or around 15 July 1995 in Dutch that I gave to my head of section 2/3.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And what is section 2/3, sir?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS
utterances.text: In the battalion staff we had an officer responsible for operation and intelligence, and I gave it to him. S2 is intelligence; S3 is operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. So typically those are two separate cells, and in this case, is it fair to say it was one person performing both jobs?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. I think we are done with this document for now.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. President, are we technically capable of looking at -- of having LiveNote and regular e-court? Or are we -- we're still down. Okay. Well, let's look at P1164. And with the Court's permission, we'll just proceed then by talking about what we have in front of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, we are looking at an English translation on the left-hand of the screen. Is that a translation of the Dutch document that we just saw on the ELMO?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. And you were shown these documents in the Popovic case, and I just wanted to go over a couple of matters with you. If we look at paragraph 5, the question is: "Did you observe the selection of refugees by the BSA? Please describe." And your answer was: "Yes, all the men were gathered near a house. I was there. Reassured and told them that they would also be taken off to Kladanj. Unfortunately this was not carried out." You testified in the Krstic case --

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And just for the record, this is at transcript pages 2886 to 2887.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: -- that you believed at the time what you were told by these Serb soldiers, that these men and boys in the white house would be taken, as the women, children, and elderly had been, to Kladanj. And you suggested in your testimony in Popovic that you may have been naive at the time. Can you please elaborate on that just a little bit for the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS
utterances.text: The men were in a state of panic and they were happy I was there, and I was trying to reassure them by asking the Bosnian Serb lieutenant what was going to happen with them. And in response, they told that first they would see exactly who these men were and that they would then be sent to Kladanj. And, of course, I looked at it, being trained in the Geneva Convention, that you treat people humanely, and I tried to reassure these people by sharing the story that I had been told with them. And when they shook their head and moved their finger from ear to ear along their throats, they were trying to tell me that it was otherwise. And although I was able to escort their wives and children up to Kladanj in the packed buses, from what I understand it didn't happen on this transport. The escort, after a while, with the weapons on the head was removed from the transport by the Bosnian Serbs, with the weapon point at the heads, and he couldn't tell me what else happened with these buses. What I saw in the house were rooms filled with men, boys, old men, who were being gathered there while their wives and children were sent on to the buses. That made a deep impression on me.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I understand that other folks in the courtroom might not be able to see what I am seeing. Okay. I am looking at a transcript at page 19, line 3, and it reads --

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And I don't know if you have it in front of you, sir: "The escort, after a while, with the weapons on the head was removed from the transport with the Bosnian heads with the weapon point at the heads and he wouldn't tell me what else happened with these buses." I think something got lost along the way, sir, to the transcript. Can you just, please, clarify, maybe repeat your answer. What you are talking about in this portion of your answer?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS
utterances.text: You want me to start at the beginning?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: No. If you could just tell us what you were referring to with the escort, and apparently there was a weapon pointed at somebody's head along the way, and if you could just share that portion of your answer with the Trial Chamber, because it didn't come out intelligibly on the transcript for some reason. What happened to the DutchBat escort who tried to escort the bus with the men and boys to Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS
utterances.text: That convoy was escorted by Lieutenant Versteeg, V-e-r-s-t-e-e-g, Versteeg. And he told me that a gun was pointed at his head and that he had to return when the transport rode on.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And just for the Trial Chamber's convenience, that very far, Lieutenant Michel Versteeg is witness number 28 in this case, whose testimony has been accepted pursuant to Rule 92 bis, so his testimony is available for the Court's review. Now, if we could just go to the next page in both versions, please, and I think we will actually have to advance one more in each.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I am afraid that we don't have the right spelling of the name of this officer on the record. The name is, in fact, V-e-r-s-t-e-e-g, Versteeg.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, again, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Now it's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir what we have here on the screen, hopefully what you are looking at as well, on the right-hand side is the English translation of the report that you spoke about a few moments ago that you saw in the original Dutch on the ELMO that you wrote on or about the 15th of July, 1995; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. And I, again, just note for the record there is a translation error. In the heading on the English it should read, "Head of S2/4," not head of "S2/34." I think that comports with what Colonel Egbers told us when he was looking at the original Dutch version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We have this number in both versions, in the B/C/S and in the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, I see it's been replicated.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, just to make one matter clear from the Popovic case. If we look at paragraphs 6, 7, and 8 of your report, and I am not going to ask you to recount what this information is in these paragraphs, but can you tell the Trial Chamber, please, what was the source of the information in paragraphs 6, 7, and 8? Who or what was the source of this information?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS
utterances.text: As I said regarding paragraph 6, I am recounting what Major Zoran - as I called him at that time - told me. I am recounting what Major Zoran told me. Major Zoran Malinic, born in 1961, is the source of the story.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And who was the source for the information in paragraphs 7 and 8 as well, sir?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS
utterances.text: That information is from the same major.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And if we look at paragraph 10, you have reported here that you met with Colonel Beara, told him what had happened, which had been written down, and you note that Colonel Beara has the originally, a copy is held by section 2/3. What you are referring to here in this paragraph 10, what is the document?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS
utterances.text: When I arrived at the school, I asked for the highest ranking officer, and I wanted to make an arrangement with him to be able to share our opinion and our feelings with him. I was received by a soldier speaking -- who spoke Serbo-Croat and English, and he advised me to draft a joint document in which I stated on behalf of the United Nations what was wrong, such as driving through the forest in an armoured vehicle. On the front of the armoured vehicle was a Dutch sergeant, and he had to call out to the Muslims in the forest that it was safe and that they should come to him. I also reported the stolen and used vehicles, uniforms, and helmets. There was no longer any difference between true UN soldiers and Bosnian Serb warriors. We wrote that down and I presented that to Colonel Beara. I -- I submitted the copy to my own section 2/3, and I never saw it again.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And, sir, did you become aware that at some period of time following the take-over of the enclave by the VRS forces, that members of DutchBat destroyed sensitive documents and other materials so that they would not fall into the hands of the VRS forces?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS
utterances.text: I saw that. They burned a lot.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: So have you ever actually seen a copy since the day you submitted that copy of the complaint to your S2/S3, have you ever seen a copy of that since?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS
utterances.text: Never again.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And how did the document that we saw on the ELMO a little while ago in Dutch, the report, this 15 July report that we are looking at the translation of now, how did that make it out of the enclave?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS
utterances.text: I brought that with me, myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, at this time I would formally move to, I guess, add the Dutch original that actually forms the basis of the document that's already been admitted to our Rule 65 ter list of exhibits and tender it along with the B/C/S and English translations which already exist.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The Dutch original is already admitted?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: No, no. The Dutch original is what I am moving to admit. It forms the basis of the English translation and the B/C/S translations which have already been admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And I take it this is uploaded into e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: It is now, actually, as we were -- as we were working it made it onto the system.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And I think it can retain the same 65 ter number if you think that makes it easy for everybody.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Indeed. And this will be admitted into evidence all together, the Dutch original, the English, and the B/C/S translation as P1164.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Now, if we may have P1167 on e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, can you tell the Trial Chamber what this document is that we are looking at?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS
utterances.text: This is a witness statement that I made on 24 October, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And if we could scroll down just a little bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Do you recognise your signature anywhere on this page?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS
utterances.text: My signature appears at the left.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I note for the record that the English version of this statement has been admitted as P1145, and there is a B/C/S translation of that, naturally. What we are looking at now was not admitted in the Popovic case, although it was shown to the witness. What I'd like to do is ask Colonel Egbers to look at a couple of the attachments to this, one of which was also shown to him in the Popovic case. So if we could go to page 10 in the e-court, please, we will be looking at two sketches so there is no translation as yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Do you see a sketch, sir, before you?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. We can see a circle at the bottom right-hand with some letters and then some other markings. Can you please just take a moment and explain to the Trial Chamber what this sketch shows; and there is also some Dutch, and if you would kindly translate some of the Dutch portions for the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS
utterances.text: The circle at the bottom of the sheet of paper depicts the enclave Srebrenica with some observation posts. The line directed toward Bratunac depicts the road to Bratunac. Then if you look from the word "Bratunac" to the left, the road continues, and I've indicated during the interrogation that the road was filled with Bosnian Serb soldiers. It reads "four loops [phoen]," that's a piece of anti-aircraft weapon with four barrels pointed at the forest. Just a bit further on --

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Let me just stop you for a minute because we are going to do a little bit of marking and translating as we go. So if you would take the stylist, there should be a little magic pen with the court assistant's help here. Ah, you got it. Okay. You just referred to four lopes loops, or an anti-aircraft gun. If you could just circle what you are referring to and maybe write AA gun next to that so we know what you are talking about, please.

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. And we can see a lot of little circles that are -- you've drawn on along the roads and some arrows pointing in various directions. Can you tell the Trial Chamber what those little circles are?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS
utterances.text: Those little small circles depict groups of up to three soldiers, and the arrow is the direction of their line of vision. They were focussing in the direction of the enclave, that's what they were looking at.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. And sir, if you would, please continue describing what you've drawn here. And if you think it helps to mark additionally any of the elements, please do.

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS
utterances.text: I would like to apologise for this unclear drawing, but I didn't realise that I was going to need to explain it 15 years later. Past the anti-aircraft gun, I've written: "Roadblock Konjevici." The road was closed off there and we had to turn left in our vans. The road from Konjevici to Simici, that road was also filled with soldiers. There were a lot of Bosnian Serb soldiers, and again they were looking in the direction of the enclave. And I've drawn a small football field, I'll circle it, that's the Nova Kasaba football field where I saw all those men kneeling with their hands on their neck on the football field. And just a bit further I wrote down, I'll underline this school, that was where we were being held. The buses rode on toward Kladanj, and I'll underline that as well, that's where the buses stopped. The large arrow that I drew, and that's a bit strange because I wrote that in English, Muslim people, that's the direction in which the Bosnian Serb men and boys were walking toward the free Bosnian area. And, in fact, all of this is a trap, a trap by the Bosnian Serb soldiers to catch the Muslim men.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Let me just stop you right there, sir. I think I heard you say that that arrow represented the Bosnian Serb men and boys walking to the free Bosnian area. Did you mean Bosnian Serb men and boys or something else?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS
utterances.text: I meant the refugees that were in Srebrenica and independently walked to Tuzla, or, in any case, the free area, and those were the Muslim youths and men.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. And just lastly, the -- in the upper right-hand corner, there is something written in Dutch, and if you would kindly just translate what you've written there. Or, perhaps, just read it in Dutch and the translators will do it for us.

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS
utterances.text: I -- the English word doesn't come to mind, but a "fauk [phoen]" is something -- so a trap or a net in this case, that's something that fish swim into, and I hope our interpreters can interpret that properly.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: In the context mentioned by the speaker, it is a net, says the translator.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. And what else have you written here?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS
utterances.text: It reads: "Net by BSA, Bosnian Serb army, to catch BiH, Muslim men."

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, Colonel. That was very helpful.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: If we could save this document now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received, but I would clarify the situation. The original sketch was an attachment to the document P1167 or P1145. In fact, what is the difference between these two documents?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: It's attached originally to P1167, which is the Dutch language original witness statement. When the statement was translated into English, the sketches didn't carry over, that's why we have to work with the Dutch original because that's the version that has the sketches attached to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And we want to receive the number of the marked sketch.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P1302 [Realtime transcript read in error "P10002"], Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think we have not the right number on the screen. Perhaps it can be repeated.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, the number is P1302 [Realtime transcript read in error "P1032"].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think it's again wrong, 1302. Thank you. We have still a problem with e-court. There is no connection on some screens, only one Judge is in the position to follow the transcript, not the other two judges. I don't know what is happening here, but Mr. Thayer, please carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. If we could go to the next page in the document, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I am not going to ask you to go into too much detail about this sketch, Colonel. Can you just tell the Trial Chamber who drew it and who made the markings in English?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS
utterances.text: This is also my handwriting. I drew and wrote this on 24 October, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And without going into the particulars, because I think they are pretty self-explanatory, can you just tell the Trial Chamber what this sketch depicts?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS
utterances.text: At the top you see the road from Simici to Konjevici -- may I writes on this?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS
utterances.text: I am circling the roadblock. Here I am circling the roadblock that stopped all our vehicles. The vehicles were parked there on the square. Here men and boys were being held. I already stated there. We were staying at the school, whereas here dogs were held. On the square were mortars and Bosnian Serb armoured personnel carriers.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And you just referred to some dogs. Can you tell the Trial Chamber what you were able to observe about the dogs that were at this location? For what purpose could you discern that these dogs were present?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS
utterances.text: They were German shepherds, aggressive dogs, used by the servicemen. I saw similar dogs days earlier in the enclave in the house by Pusmulici, I am not sure whether they were the same dogs.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And did it appear to you that these dogs were part of the military unit that was headquartered here or were they part of some other unit, from what you could see?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS
utterances.text: They were part of the unit of that Major Zoran.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, Colonel. I think we can save this document and move to the next one, please. When we get the number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This marked sketch will be received as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P1303 [Realtime transcript read in error "P10303"], Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think we have again a problem with the number of this document.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. The number again is P1303.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please carry, Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. If we could turn to the next page, please. And may I proceed, Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, please, carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Colonel, we have a sketch in front of us. Again, the heading is "Nova Kasaba." Please tell the Trial Chamber who made these markings and whose writing is on this sketch?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS
utterances.text: This is not my handwriting but that of the person who interrogated me. I did sign it at the bottom right of this page.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And again without going into too much detail, can you please tell the Trial Chamber, just generally speaking, what does this sketch depict?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS
utterances.text: You see two vehicles driving north along the football field, a large bus with refugees, and behind that my Mercedes, and the little dot is me. To the right is a football field where Muslim men and youths were kneeling, and people, Muslim men and youth, along the road on their way to the football field. And on the football field I saw about 20 soldiers and a table. I was driving at 40 to 45 kilometres an hour along this football field. I was riding behind the bus.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, Colonel, in your Popovic testimony you stated that you passed by this football field on more than one occasion on the 12th and 13th of July. When we see here on the sketch where its written: "Almost whole field covered with people," was that the case for all the occasions when you saw this football field; for example, the first time on the 12th, or did it apply to the 13th or both? If you could just tell the Trial Chamber or give the Trial Chamber some indication when the football field was almost completely covered with people.

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS
utterances.text: That was the first time I drove past it on the first day of the deportation. Later on, it was not as full any more.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay, Mr. President. The Prosecution would tender P1167.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received. And I would like to ask the witness one question related to the sketch on the screen. You told us that we can see your signature on this page and the handwriting was done by the person who interviewed you. Who made this the sketch itself, the football field in the street and the cars?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am not entirely certain anymore whether she did that or I did that, but in any case it's exactly as I remember it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I see we're coming up on the break and I am about to start a new series of questions, so with the Court's indulgence, if we could take the break now that would be convenient.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This is a good proposal. Has everybody the transcript in e-court again on the screen? All problems solved, Mr. Gajic? Yes, okay. That's fine. We must have our first break now and we will resume quarter past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: While we are dealing with, Colonel, your 24 October 1995 witness statement, let's look at the English translation for a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: This is P1145. And there is a B/C/S version of that as well, but if we could P1145 in e-court, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay, sir, we have here the English translation of your OTP witness statement from the 24th of October, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: If we could go to page 5 in both the English and the B/C/S version, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: There is a loud typing noise from your side. Perhaps you can use the other microphone, it could reduce the amount of noise.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Will do. Ms. Stewart is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: She's always busy.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: She's always busy.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, if we could focus on the paragraph that begins: "Convoy 3 ... ," please, there is a reference. Well, let's just take a look at the paragraph, and you refer here to another one of the convoys carrying the women, children, and elderly. You said: "I rode with Lutke again and we were last in the line. We were regularly made to stop by Bosnian Serbian soldiers. They wanted our bullet-proof vests, helmets, and weapons." And you go on. And then you state: "I heard over the radio that other vehicles were being robbed as well." Do you see that, sir, a little bit further into the paragraph? Just take a moment and let me know when you read that -- reach that point. You state that you heard radio reports that this stripping of the UN escorts was also happening to other Dutch peacekeepers. Based on your own experience and what you heard being reported, does this appear to you to be a random occurrence of stopping, stripping, disabling, the peacekeepers, or did it appear to you to be co-ordinated in some fashion?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS
utterances.text: We drove behind the bus and were in touch with each other over the radio, and I understood that all white UN vehicles were being stopped and that our helmets and bullet-proof vests were being requested. Only by pointing at my rank was I able to retain my own things. This had happened to all of us. It was not an isolated occurrence that it happened to somebody, this was carefully thought out.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now let's move to a different document if we could, please. This is P1148.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Just to save a little bit of time, sir, what we have here on the right is an English translation of a debriefing statement that you gave to the Dutch authorities. That statement, and its original form being in your own language, so what we are looking at here is the English translation. This is a statement that you gave on 11 September, 1995. Do you recall providing this debriefing statement at Assen?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, if we could go to page 4, please, of this document. And this will be page 4 in both the English and the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I want to draw your attention, Colonel, to the very first paragraph where it says: "With each new battalion, the BSA had clearly shifted the boundaries. As a result, the enclave was getting smaller all the time. As January 1995 approached, the BSA also came closer and closer to the enclave borders. After a while UNPROFOR was no longer allowed to enter the so-called Bandera Triangle. It was unclear why. "Both the Muslims and the Serbs did whatever they pleased in the Bandera Triangle. If the Serbs wanted to stop a convoy, then they did," et cetera. Can you please explain a little bit more what you were talking about here and what was going on with respect to the activity of both the Muslim fighters, or presence in the triangle, as well as the VRS presence in the Bandera Triangle.

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS
utterances.text: As you did indeed read out, it turned out that with each new battalion, the borders were once again a subject of debate. And upon our arrival in January 1995, we observed that the BSA was moving closer in the direction of the enclave. We had just arrived in the enclave and did not know how to respond to this. Then some Muslims took their own initiatives to ensure that their enclave didn't shrink further. They wanted to ensure that the Bosnian Serbs remained at a distance and through this measure deprived us of access to the Bandera Triangle. We were in there, in fact, but it's not so that Serbs and Muslims were intermingled or that it wasn't clear. The enclave border remained in effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And when you say in this briefing that both the Muslims and the Serbs did whatever they pleased in the Bandera Triangle, can you provide any examples or just provide a little bit more clarity about what you are referring to?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS
utterances.text: The Bosnian Serbs fired grenades from outside the enclave in the triangle. We heard many explosions to the south of OP Alpha, and the Muslims prevented us from getting access to that triangle so we didn't know exactly what they wanted to do over there. So it's not so much that it was unclear. The border remained in effect and was enforced. There was additional shelling by the Serbs in that triangle, and the Muslims tried to resist.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, during the VRS attack on the enclave, say from approximately 6 of July through the fall of the enclave, on or about the 11th or even the 12th of July, depending on how you look at it, did you become aware ever of any information indicating that there was any Muslim resistance, reinforcements, military activity, that was coming out of the Bandera Triangle, weapons, men streaming out of the triangle, any reports of any kind of such activity with respect to the Bandera Triangle?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS
utterances.text: No, it wasn't that way at all. The attack of the Bosnian Serbs was directed at the south of the enclave. Nothing at all was happening in that Bandera Triangle. There were no warriors or arms there. There wasn't anything there.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: If we could go to page 15 of this document, please, and that's in both versions. I want to ask you a quick question about a topic that I don't think was raised in the Popovic case.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: About three quarters of the way down the English, and it's going to be about smack in the middle of the B/C/S, there is a reference here to your return to the compound, and I take it that's your return to the Potocari compound, the Charlie Company compound. And you refer here to: "Before the lighting point, he had seen a dead woman who was probably overcome due to heat and exhaustion." Now, I am not sure you have ever been asked in the Krstic case or the Popovic case about this dead woman that you saw. If you could cast your memory back a little bit and just share with the Trial Chamber whatever you can recall about where exactly you saw this dead woman and anything he else about the circumstances.

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS
utterances.text: I escorted the first transport of buses, and all those buses stopped in the middle of the forest. We got out to see what was wrong. The very first convoy stopped and the women and children thought that they were going to be killed there. From the bus, they made motions across their neck from their left to their right ear; after all, we stopped in the middle of the forest. I tried to reassure them and they basically passed the body of the dead woman outside -- over the heads of the other women. So I walked on to the point where the buses were being unloaded further on. It was well organised. The doors of one bus opened, the women and children were told to alight and to walk on to a certain road without knowing exactly where. This happened in the forest at that border where most of the women thought that they were going to be killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Just to further orient ourselves, this is at the location from which these women, children, and elderly had to walk an additional several kilometres to get to the free territory; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And do you recall anything further about this woman who died, her approximate age, were you told anything about what caused her death?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS
utterances.text: At that point, I couldn't pay the attention to her that I would have liked to because at other points women and children had to alight, and that was a very emotional occurrence. It was about 35 degrees centigrade. She wasn't old, around 40, I believe. But as for the cause of death, I was unable to determine, but I assume it had something to do with the emotion, the heat, the tension. It could have had something to do with those factors. She wasn't -- she didn't have any gun-shot injuries or anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Let's look at another document, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: That's P1143.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Again, just to move things along a little bit, what we have here on the left is a transcript, in Dutch, of your 2 September 1999 interview with the representatives from the NIOD or NIOD organisation, the Dutch Institute for War Documentation. Do you recall providing that information, sir?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I believe there is a B/C/S translation which should be available in e-court. If not, my friends have been given a copy. There we go. Okay. If we could have page 14 in English and page 21 in the B/C/S, please. We will be looking at paragraph 206.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is in Dutch on the right.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: If we can get the B/C/S up, that'd be great, please. And in the meantime -- and again, that's page 21 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: If we look at paragraph 206, Colonel, you say: "I did see a lot of lines on the way there, a lot of communication equipment, telephone lines that went along the cliffs. About ten for sure. They did have good communication lines. Not in the air, because then they could be located. I sometimes used my radio, but the Serbs did not like that because the Muslims could locate you and then they could fire mortars at you there. They thought that the Muslims could do all that which, of course, wasn't so, and so they used land lines a lot." My question, Colonel, is when you refer to: "They having good communication lines," what you are talking about? Who is "they," and if you could give some examples of some of the communications lines that you observed and where you saw them?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What I saw was that from the school where the headquarters were and Major Zoran, communications -- communication lines ran in the direction of Nova Kasaba. And when there was any communication along these lines, this was impossible for others to tap into. So that's why military units always use these lines to communicate exclusively with each other without others eavesdropping. And my impression was that this was well organised. Many lines were deployed to different telephones.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And can you explain what, again, what the reaction was of the Serb soldiers to you when you tried to use your UN radio. What was their response? What did they tell you?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS
utterances.text: I was prohibited from doing this and a gun was pointed at me. They were all armed and they were afraid that others would be able to eavesdrop or determine their position. That's what they told me.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, going back to the period of the attack itself on the enclave from 6 to, say, 11 July, 1995, how were your communications abilities, yours personally, as a DutchBat officer, with your other units with your command, and, from what you could hear from the radio traffic, among other elements of DutchBat during this attack?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS
utterances.text: On my blocking position 1, I always had good radio contact with the captain supervising me, but I also had to ensure with my vehicle that other vehicles in the south of the enclave would be able to have contact with this commander as well. So I had radio contact and that was maintained by my vehicle radio.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, if we could go to page 17 in the English and page 26 in the B/C/S, please. We'll be looking at paragraph 264.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: If we look at paragraph 264, you say: "There was also a big threat when I came back with all those refugees. A stream of people came in. Lieutenant Versteeg stood there with a radio in order to act as backup as a forward air controller. At that point he also had to call off all the missions because the Bosnian Serbs were threatening us, not only to butcher the 30 Dutch people in Bratunac but also all the refugees and the UN personnel in Srebrenica." Can you help place when this threat occurred? Just give us a little bit of context for this threat?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS
utterances.text: On that day, I was very close to the attack by the NATO F-16s on a Bosnian Serb tank. Because the tank had stopped firing, I was able to go to the village of Srebrenica where, together with all refugees, I walked in the direction of Potocari. The mortars dropped to the left and right of the refugees walking together with us to Potocari, the 5 kilometres. When I arrived at the headquarters, I spoke with Versteeg who told me that we had to stop the air attacks immediately because otherwise we would be bombed. That's why he assigned the pilots to cease their close air support.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: So this information contained here in paragraph 264, the threat to kill the 30 Dutch people in Bratunac but also the refugees and other UN personnel, who related that threat to you?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS
utterances.text: That information came from the Bosnian Serbs. Exactly how it came to him is a mystery to me, but he was expected to carry out the assignment to cease the close air support immediately.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, if we could go to page 35 in the English, and this will be page 54 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I want to look at paragraph 586 and then put a couple of other things to you before asking you my question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The B/C/S page is not the right one. I think it must be the previous one.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. If we could go back one page. Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: You say that: "We only got permission to fire at the Serbs. When I reported that the Serbs seemed to be approaching the town of Srebrenica in a column of units, walking in a column, I was told 'Fire at them.' My guns had a range of only 800 metres and they were kilometres away. It didn't make sense." Now you testified in the Popovic trial that you never saw the order from then Major Franken through Captain Groen to use all available means to prevent a breakthrough by the VRS into the town. You never saw that order. Here you state that you had permission to fire at the Serbs and you were told to fire at the Serbs. Can you explain what your understanding of your order was at that point, what the circumstances of your situation was if you never saw what we refer to as the Groen order from Major Franken?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS
utterances.text: Major Franken put together a fax in which he formulated instructions and he sent that fax to Major Groen, as the commander of the Bravo Company in the south of the enclave. I was out in the field, not at a post, and of course I never sought that order. That's unusual. It's unusual for him to give me instructions over the radio, and this was a translation of his instruction to me in the field.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: So is it fair to say that your understanding of your assignment was the same as that contained in the Groen order but you just never saw it. You never saw the actual order, but the substance of the order was communicated to you. Is that fair to say, or do I have it wrong in some form?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS
utterances.text: That's correct. I took the question: Have you seen the orders literally, and the response to that was: No. But I did observe how Major Groen, at the time Captain Groen, translated that into instructions to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, Colonel, you testified in the Popovic trial, and this is at page 2796, and I quote: "I don't think that we were under attack by Muslim fighters." You testified in the Popovic case about Private van Renssen being killed by a Muslim fighter. You testified about your own APC coming under fire from Muslim fighters in Srebrenica town when they thought that you were withdrawing, possibly for good, your APC came under fire. Can you explain to the Trial Chamber your answer that despite those incidents, you did not believe that the UN was under attack by Muslim forces?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS
utterances.text: At Bravo 1, blocking position 1, we were positioned with two APCs. We were the only protection remaining for the Muslim warriors present there. They all -- they were all very lightly armed. You could say that all they had were rifles. They never threatened me, but one of them, perhaps in a moment of panic, shot at our vehicle when we were assigned to proceed to the city of Srebrenica. The strange thing is that the board gunner of our vehicle is not armoured, so he was unprotected on top. That's how it was decided. That made him very vulnerable, just like Raviv van Renssen who died because of one of warriors wanted to keep the vehicle there and responded that way. I did not feel threatened by the Muslim warriors, more so by the Bosnian warriors who fired at us with tanks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: May I ask what you mean by "Bosnian warriors," in your last sentence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Those are the refugees in the enclave with a rifle.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. I think matters got us slightly more confused there.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Colonel, and I'm just looking at the transcript, the transcript reads: "I did not feel threatened by the Muslim warriors, more so by the Bosnian warriors who fired at us with tanks." I guess my first question is: Who had the tanks?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS
utterances.text: I used the word "Bosnian Serb," but perhaps it would be better to say Serb in this case, or BSA, the tanks were in the hands of the Bosnian Serbs. They fired at us. And I was also fired at by a Muslim warrior with a rifle, but I didn't feel threatened by that. When I arrived in the city of Srebrenica, where thousands of refugees, men, women, a big jumble, were I mounted the vehicle to show that we were staying there and that we would not all retreat to safety.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Judge Nyambe has a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Thank you. On page 43, line 6 to 7, Mr. Thayer is reading to you a portion from a previous transcript where you are reported to have said: "I did not feel threatened by the Muslim warriors, more so by the Bosnian warriors who fired at us with tanks." Can you just clarify for me, were these -- does this relate to the incident where a DutchBat soldier was killed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There was -- earlier there was just a reference to the killing of Raviv van Renssen, the Dutch soldier who was killed in the enclave. I wasn't present there. All I can do is say what I have heard about that. What happened to me was that with an APC I drove from my blocking position to Srebrenica, and the armoured vehicle was shot at with a rifle there, and the board gunner sustained mild injured in that incident, but it's not comparable to the shooting by the Bosnian Serbs, or the firing by the Bosnian Serbs with tanks, at our location.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Okay. So you are saying the incident referred there is not the same as the incident you were involved in here?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was involved, when I read 586, I -- we are talking about 586, aren't we?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Yes, we are, just to clarify, two things, we are referring to paragraph 586 of the NIOD statement, and maybe I can clarify one matter. The portion that I was quoting to the witness, and I'll quote it again: "I did not feel threatened by the Muslim warriors, more so by the Bosnian warriors who fired at us with tanks." That portion is of a transcript that just appeared a few moments ago. And if I'm not mistaken, that was an incorrectly interpreted answer from the witness. So we are not talking about, as I understand it, any Bosnian Muslims with tanks. I -- if I understand it, Colonel Egbers has clarified that he's referring to Bosnian Serb forces with tanks. Maybe we can start there and then get back to 586 to help you answer the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: First of all, just so the record is completely clear, were you ever referring in your answer to Bosnian Muslim forces with tanks?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS
utterances.text: No, I didn't do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And the incidents that you've testified about today where your APCs did come under light arms fire by Muslim fighters, you said that you weren't -- you didn't feel threatened by that, but those incidents were separate from the incident in which Raviv van Renssen was killed by Muslim fighters; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And turning back to the paragraph 586, when you refer to being ordered to fire at the Serb column that you saw approaching Srebrenica, can you give us some idea in terms of, if not the actual date, if you can't remember the actual date, that's okay, but approximately how many days after Private van Renssen's death did the events in paragraph 586 occur?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS
utterances.text: I believe that's two days later.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And he's back in Your Honour's hand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I am sorry for the intervention. I just wanted to make it clear because I don't think I had made it clear enough what I was quoting from when I quoted from that prior answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: I appreciate your explanation, actually. It clears some confusion in my mind. I still have one question for the witness. The attack on your APC came two days after the DutchBat soldier Renssen was fired at and killed, and you still did not feel threatened by this attack on your APC two days later?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS
utterances.text: Of course I was very shocked by the death of a soldier from our unit, but my assignment was to put up a blocking position elsewhere, coincidentally in the same area where the Bosnian Muslim warriors were and I started by contacting them. I did not feel threatened by them. I even asked them not to fire because otherwise the Bosnian Serbs would think that I had fired at them and they obeyed. The piece of mortar that was hidden there was never fired.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Thank you very much for your clarification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Judge Mindua has a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We don't have interpretation at the moment.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Is it better now? Can you hear us? Can you hear the English interpretation on the English channel? Thank you very much. Sorry. Could the Judge, please, repeat the question. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, I would like to ask a question regarding the terminology you used. Up until today we are kind of used to the term VRS, that is the BSA Army in English, and we are used to the terms ABiH, so the army of the Muslims of Bosnia. One witness came to testify and talked about Muslims, civilian Muslims, who took place in an incident which caused the death of soldier van Renssen. However, today you also talked about Muslim warriors, so Muslim soldiers, and you also talked to us about Bosnian warriors. You told us that you were attacked by a tank of -- filled with Bosnian warriors, so I would just like to make sure I understood you correctly. When you were talking about Bosnian soldiers, or warriors as you mentioned, you are talking about the VRS or the BSA, so the Serb Bosnian army, I guess. So if that is the case, when you are talking about Muslim warriors or combatants or soldiers, are you talking, in fact, about Muslim civilians, the same people mentioned by that particular witness, or are you actually talking about the ABiH? Now we are faced with four different terms, so that's just what I wanted to clarify. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The men in the enclave were not a military unit as we know them to be in western countries. There were many refugees gathered but those -- that did not make them soldiers. Some were armed but that doesn't make them an army or a brigade or a division. Although the Bosnian Muslims, the BiH, told with pride about their huge fighting forces in the enclave. That was only propaganda. They had nothing. The men who were wandering around there with rifles were not organised. When I consider the Bosnian Serb army, the BSA, they all had uniforms, tanks, communication devices, that was an army in the enclave. They were refugees with -- who were armed. I can't attribute the same status to them as to the Bosnian Serb army. They communicated through notes and pencils, and when the Bosnian Serbs started the attack on the enclave in the south, they openly started wearing uniforms and bearing arms hoping to be able to do something against the attack, but they didn't have anything. You really can't call it an army.
