utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Witness. I understood your answer. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Judge Nyambe again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Just to follow-up on the question from Judge Mindua, and really this is a hypothetical question. Suppose there was a unit of soldiers who were suddenly - how shall I put it? - who are suddenly without a leader, without uniforms, wandering around but armed, what would you call that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, you could see that at the moment in question. When there was an attack on the enclave, they will act in a structured manner and that's not the case. What I saw was a number of willing and able young men taking rifles to the south from blocking position 1 to try to neutralise a tank. Most men later assembled in the north of the enclave to break out, but there was no pattern or structure in the enclave that was visible to us. We knew who the military points of contact were, but you can't compare that to a real army in which soldiers are trained and armed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: No, I am just trying to understand the -- sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Pardon, pardon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Oh, I can continue. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Dutch on English channel]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Stop for a moment. We have here now the Dutch translation. We have heard the Dutch interpretation. Hopefully we are back now on the English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Yes, I just wanted you to explain for me the new terminology that has been introduced that Judge Mindua has referred to in describing what was happening in the enclave. Is the term "warrior" meant to cover, for example, the hypothetical question I've put to you, a band of former soldiers may be confused, running around, are those the ones you are calling warriors? Or who are the warriors you are referring to, basically?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am referring to refugees who were given rifles and had to join the fighting without military training or uniforms but who did their best to defend the enclave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer, you get the floor back, but I would like to note that you already used more than two hours instead of one hour you have indicated before the witness appeared in court.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I am --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Go ahead, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: -- painfully cognisant of that fact, Mr. President. I am winding down. I do feel like I am wading in molasses, but I think again that, if I may say so, that some of these issues are central issues to not only to Colonel Egbers's Popovic testimony that we are fleshing out and that's why I have gone into those topics, because even after a second or third review of the Popovic transcript of his testimony, some matters can still not make sense, and that's one of the reasons why I want to go over some of the these areas, but I am winding down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I am not worrying about the content of your questions but the length. This is -- of course the Chamber has to make clear that we should try to be as speedy as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I will do my best, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Based on your -- just following up on some of the questions from the Trial Chamber, Colonel, based on your observations, based on your experience in the enclave, the men who you described as willing and able to do their part to defend the enclave, based on what you saw, were those men capable of handling, let's say that they had been armed with more sophisticated weaponry, or let's say that they had been armed with more weaponry, based on what you had seen in terms of their training and military abilities, would they have been able to make good use of that equipment? And my second question again, I am sorry to but two in one, but my second question is: Did you see any evidence of these willing and able soldiers being armed to the teeth, armed with sophisticated weaponry, every willing and able-bodied men armed with some type of weapon? Did you see that yourself?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS
utterances.text: No. I saw refugees who dug trenches and later walked about armed to ensure that the attack would stop, but from my point of view that's not an army. And I apologise for the confusion that I caused, but there was an army outside the enclave, the Bosnian Serbs. Inside were refugees, some of whom were armed. But from my professional perspective, they did not constitute an army, they were not a force, they do not communicate with one another, and they were poorly armed. Did this answer your questions sufficiently?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I think at this point I would actually ask the Honourable Judge Nyambe just to make sure that, Your Honour, that your question was answered sufficiently. I think some of the follow-up questions I had were trying to get at the nub of Your Honour's question in terms of what you would call whatever the forces were that you saw constituting the Bosnian Muslim resistance to the VRS. You've said it wasn't an army, what would you call it if there -- if you do have a word that you would call it, if you don't then, okay, but if there is a word that sort of captures how you would describe them in one word, what would that word be?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We don't receive interpretation at the moment.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A group of men, some of them in uniforms, some of them armed with small calibre weapons, as they are called, so rifles, some of them had an RPG, but far too few in number to do anything against an organised army. Basically they were armed refugees.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: If we could go to page 38 in the English, which is page 58 in the B/C/S. This will be our last paragraph in this document. And actually we will need to see the Dutch version for a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I am very sorry I have to interrupt you again, Mr. Thayer. Judge Mindua has a question related to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am sorry I have to intervene once again. I hope this is my last question for this witness today. Witness, what you have just said is very important for me in view of the things that we have discussed so far. When we are talking about combatants or civilians who were disarmed, they didn't have their own structure, they didn't have -- they didn't undergo military training. You, as a military commander, you belonged to an army where you were properly trained, and you also had appropriate equipment. How would you react if you asked to restore peace within the armed civilians --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues] ... the military care about structure. The military care about structure. I am waiting a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Now we don't have French interpretation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The military care about structure, there should be leadership.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Now it's working.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They should be armed, not only with rifles, but to prevent an attack on the enclave, they should have mortars, tanks, thousands of soldiers to protect that. They need to be trained and there should be communication devices within the enclave. And I didn't see any of those. The commander of the artillery device at blocking position 1 wrote a brief note to Ramiz with my request that the artillery device not be used. That's what he had. So from my perspective, there was no organised army in the enclave, but there was outside the enclave. The Bosnian Serbs of course did have that tank, communication devices, uniforms, training.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for your answer, but I think we were talking at cross-purposes here. This was a hypothetical case. You are a military commander. On your side you had an organised army and equipment, and on the other side there was a population, a civilian population, among whom some were armed. And in this hypothetical example -- for example, you are asked, you, as a military commander, to restore order. How would you react? Would you apply military measures of the kind that you would apply among your own troops? That's my question, and it's rather hypothetical, I agree.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If there were armed civilians who were not organised, you can't regard them as an army. And, of course, throughout the world there were armed citizens and they will have to be disarmed when a conflict arises in a certain region. And it's difficult to say how you would do that in practice in a hypothetical situation. Disarming is a separate project, and you would need to contact the representatives of that civilian population and ask them to organise that. There are different opportunities, not merely military ones, and that hypothetical situation conceivably it might be agreed how we should proceed. But if I may be so free as to refer to the conflict where I was present, that didn't happen there and they were fired at with tanks, mortars, and their houses were set on fire. The people were driven -- they were driven away.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer, back to you again.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Just quickly to follow-up on His Honour Judge Mindua's question, can you tell the Trial Chamber what efforts DutchBat was able to take to disarm people with guns inside the enclave that patrols, for example, would encounter in the field or in town?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS
utterances.text: From January until June 1995 there were many patrols of the UN soldiers in the enclave to see whether any weapons remained. If we saw people who were armed, we would pursue them into their houses to confiscate their arms and to hand them over to the manager of the weapon collection point in Srebrenica. Patrols went out daily with these instructions. Only when the attack on the enclave was launched did the Muslims bear their arms openly.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And how successful would you characterise the peacekeeper's efforts at seizing these weapons that you should occasionally see people in Srebrenica bearing? You had testified that they had run into their homes, for example. How successful overall would you say DutchBat was in disarming, to that degree, those who were armed in the enclave?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS
utterances.text: If we saw their arms, we would act, but at the end of the enclave it turned out that there were many arms that we hadn't seen or they were being brought into the enclave at that point. But we did what we could, we couldn't do any more than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, back to P1143. Great. We will need to go back one page in the Dutch, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, I would like you just to read paragraph 624 into the record. I think when we met, you noted that there was a somewhat significant error in the English translation of this portion. So I just want to straighten that out, so if you would please read paragraph 624 into the record.

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS
utterances.text: "Only of that Versteeg, who was at the compound, and of others who heard the threats of the BSA that mortars would fire at us from Bratunac, those are the only effects that I heard. And, however, I did hear mortar fire to the left and to the right of the refugees. They kept on firing to, as it were, keep people going."

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, my first question, sir, is: With respect to the mortar fire that you've testified about in Popovic and you've spoken about today, to the left and right of the column of refugees fleeing from Srebrenica to Potocari, did you just hear that mortar fire or did you actually see it landing yourself?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS
utterances.text: I both heard and saw it.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. And in this last sentence here where it reads in the English translation: "They continued to shell in order to stop the movement, as it were." I take it that's the direct opposite of what is in the original Dutch version which is: "They continued to shell in order to keep the column moving." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS
utterances.text: That is correct. It says, "They kept on shelling to keep it moving, as it were."

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And do you stand by that statement, sir? Is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS
utterances.text: Of course I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Just a couple more questions for you, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: But first, Mr. President, I would like to tender P1143 before I forget.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, somewhat related to this passage that we just read from your NIOD statement, in the Krstic case, and this is at transcript page 2214 if anybody is following that, you testified with respect to the VRS shelling of Srebrenica town, you testified, and I quote: "I think they wanted to scare the refugees who were in the city of Srebrenica so that they would go north to Potocari and they could enter the town. They were scaring them, and, of course, they were wounding them, killing them."

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS
utterances.text: Was that a question?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I just wanted to make sure you got the translation.

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. My first question is: Do you stand by that testimony? Is that testimony accurate and do you stand by it?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, based on the shelling which you observed from Bravo 1 from your other observations being in the town itself, what options did the civilian population in Srebrenica town have in terms of where it could go?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS
utterances.text: Only to Potocari.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And, again, why? What was happening that made Potocari the only place that those civilians could go?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS
utterances.text: Because thousands of people were in the village of Srebrenica on the market-place and the mortars were being fired by the Bosnian Serbs or there was firing of different things, so the only road free to them was the road to the north to Potocari. The road to the south was, of course, closed by the Bosnian Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I thank you, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I have no further questions at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think the last sentence of the answer was not complete. The road to the south was, of course? And there is a word missing. I think I heard "closed." Perhaps you can clarify it with the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Colonel, I don't know if you heard the Presiding Judge's intervention, and I don't know if you have the transcript in front of you to see exactly what he's referring to, but is there a missing word in your last answer, at least in terms of the transcript that you can clarify.

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS
utterances.text: Of course the people could no longer go to the south because the Bosnian Serbs were there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: So what was the case in terms of the road? Just to clarify that. The transcript reads: "The road to the south was ..." and then there is nothing.

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS
utterances.text: Closed [Interpretation] Closed.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Judge Nyambe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: I just have one more question for the witness. Correct me if I am wrong, but my understanding of your testimony is that you disarmed the population, the Muslim population, and put their arms in a secure area. Do you know whether these demobilised Muslim soldiers left the enclave or stayed in the enclave?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The weapon collection point where the arms of the Muslims were stored existed before we started working in the enclave. In the past, as agreed, weapons were surrendered there and maintained by the Muslims who surrendered them or handed them over, or where those men or women were I can't tell you that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, now it's your turn with your cross-examination. I just want to note that we didn't receive a list of documents you are going to use during the cross-examination. Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, we have not submitted the list because we intended to use only the documents provided by the OTP in their list. However, given the nature of this witness's testimony, and especially in its part, in the course of the evening we will submit a list of some 10 or 15 documents that we intend to use with this witness tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I would like to greet everybody in the courtroom including this witness. May God's peace reign in this house and may God's will and not mine be done in these proceedings. Since no documents have been submitted, as Mr. Gajic as just told you, we are going to use the witness's statement, number P1145 which was tendered by the OTP and which has its translation. Could the Court please produce P1145 in e-court. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please see the second page of the statement to give the witness an opportunity to see what I am going to ask him. Thank you. Could we please focus on paragraph 2, lines 7, 8, and 9 on page 2. Page 2, paragraph 2, lines 7, 8, and 9. We can see that on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And we are talking about your statement, sir, number P1145. You said in your statement at the beginning of paragraph 2: "On Saturday, in July 8 1995, soldier van Renssen died from a bullet wound in his neck." I just read out this sentence to indicate the beginning of the passage that I am interested in. Now you look at the lines 7, 8, and 9, where you say as follows: "We did that because we wanted to find the location of Bosnian Serbs and the Muslim fighters, and also to see where the confrontation line was." My question is this, sir --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. My question is this: Can you tell us why was it that on the 8th of July, in the evening, you checked the positions of the Army of Republika Srpska and the positions of the Bosnian Army as you stated in lines 7, 8, and 9 of your statement? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS
utterances.text: That evening, I drove in my APC to the south and my instructions were to check whether Bosnian Serbs had penetrated further into the enclave and how the Muslims had responded if that were indeed the case. And my instructions were also to avoid becoming involved in any defensive position, that was why I was driving to the south.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Further on in line 10, below line 9, you say this: "About 4 kilometres before these posts, hand-grenades were thrown between our vehicles by the Muslim fighters." I am going to read one more sentence: "I know they were Muslim fighters because they were not wearing uniforms and because it was still Muslim territory." Could you please explain where this activity took place. You said that that was about 4 kilometres before the post. Which post was it, 4 kilometres before the Muslim post or 4 kilometres after the Muslim post or 4 kilometres before the posts of the Serbian Army? Could you please be more precise and tell us what you meant when you stated this?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS
utterances.text: We drove from the city of Srebrenica to the south, and approximately 4 kilometres before the observation posts inside the enclave this incident occurred.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Your microphone.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Please, could you tell us why did that incident take place and why did Muslims throw hand-grenades at your vehicles? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS
utterances.text: That evening in the south of the enclave there was heavy shooting. We were not warring parties in this. The white UN vehicles were not involved in the fighting that was in progress in the south. Why the two Muslims threw hand-grenades at my vehicle is a mystery to me. I would imagine, but then I am speculating, that it was because the rising tensions in the south at that time and the first armoured vehicle that had left the observation post in the direction of Potocari.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. We are talking about the 8th of July when soldier van Renssen died, they threw grenades at you again. And you say that after that you returned. You say that: They returned and we headed for the Bravo Company in Srebrenica. Did the Muslims want to intimidate you? Why were they attacking you? Why you, given the fact that you were there to defend their positions? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS
utterances.text: I don't know why they threw them. It was an act by an individual Muslim. I reported it and received new instructions to go to blocking position 1. It may relate to the fact that several armoured vehicles, at least one in any case, with the soldier van Renssen were riding in the direction of Potocari so that nobody else was involved in their Defence in the south.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Was your task to defend the Muslim positions in the south? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS
utterances.text: Which Muslim positions are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I am talking about the positions from which Muslims had thrown grenades at you when soldier van Renssen died and when they hit your two tanks. Were you there holding a position with those two tanks or were you just passing by? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: It's Monday afternoon court, Your Honour. We have had a lot of glitches. I am not sure what's responsible for this one, but I am not sure there has been any reference to any two tanks by either the witness or, until now, by General Tolimir. It may be an interpretation issue or something else, but I don't think there has been any reference to tanks, so if we could have some clarification about what General Tolimir is referring to, I think that would be helpful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Thayer, for jogging my memory. Those were not tanks. They were two APCs that were targeted by the Muslims and they threw grenades between them. The witness stated that. I can remind you well.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Tell me, why did they throw grenades between your two APCs, why did they kill soldier van Renssen, why did they open fire at you? Why did they do all that, whereas you did not fight them? On the contrary, you had been given the green light to fight against the Serbs. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS
utterances.text: On 8th July, we had not received any green light. I was en route to the south of the enclave to see where exactly the Bosnian Serbs might have entered the enclave. While I was en route, Muslim warriors -- Muslims, did indeed throw a hand-grenade among our APCs. Why they did that is something I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. You confirm that they did throw grenades, just as you stated in line 10. I was supposed to tell you exactly where you stated that but now you have confirmed that you know where you stated it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We must have our second break now, Mr. Tolimir. We will assume quarter past 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tolimir. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Awhile ago I asked you the question: Why did the Muslims start killing you as of the 8th and to target you with weapons, although you had not provoked them in any way, you had not deserved it from them in any way, as it were. Does this mean perhaps that the Muslims resorted to terror in order to force you to move in front of them towards the VRS?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS
utterances.text: You're asking me why they started killing us. I note that one of our soldiers was indeed killed, probably by a grenade thrown by a Muslim warrior. I was not present at that point but I was told that the observation post was fired at by a Serb tank, that they were barely able to leave the observation post and that, perhaps, the Muslims in the surroundings of the observation post thought that they were on their own. When facing Serb tanks, you're alone in that case. Later that evening, when I drove to the south in my armoured vehicle to see whether there might be a roadblock somewhere, two grenades did, indeed, fall in between my armoured vehicles. I was able to drive back to the compound of the Bravo Company and received different instructions. If you ask me why these Muslims tried to keep us in the south, all I can answer is that probably your tanks in the south of the enclave were the reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Was it perhaps the case that the Muslims had the intention of attacking the UNPROFOR in order to elicit a reaction; namely, their airforce targeting Serb positions? Do you think that there was anything that was indicative of that?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS
utterances.text: I've seen that men dressed in civilian attire in the enclave threw those grenades at me. They were very clearly Muslims, so I can't imagine that they hoped we would think that they were Bosnian Serbs. The answer is, therefore, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Fine, thank you. We are talking about the Muslims at this point, whom you saw near your positions, and you say on page 3 -- or, rather, on page 2 of this statement, the first paragraph, lines 18 to 21, I will quote it for you. You say: "That evening and that night, we noticed different groups of Muslim fighters in the area. Generally speaking, they wore camouflage uniforms or Ukrainian uniforms. They had bought the uniforms in Zepa from some Ukrainians. I saw that they were carrying AK-47, Kalashnikovs, and machine-guns. The groups were moving in a north-westerly direction away from the enclave." My question is: Did you have information before that they bought weapons and uniforms from Ukrainian soldiers in Zepa, or was that the first time that you noticed that?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS
utterances.text: That was the first time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Were all the Muslims in the position which you have described wearing such uniforms and carrying such weapons which they had procured in this way? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I didn't object the first time that the question was asked, but I need to now just to clarify matters. General Tolimir asked the question at page 64, line 24: "My question is: Did you have information before that they bought weapons and uniforms from Ukrainian soldiers in Zepa, or is that the first time that you noticed that?" And the witness answered. Up to that point there had been no indication in the statement. The portion of the statement with which the witness affirmed dealt solely with uniforms. And there was no information about any weapons being sold or bought -- sold by the Ukrainians or bought by the Muslims from the Ukrainians. I let that go. But then it's incorporated again into this next question, so I would ask to make sure that the witness understands that he's being asked two questions, one about uniforms and one about weapons, and whether he has any information about actual weapons being purchased from the Ukrainians by the Bosnians.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Presiding Judge. I am not quite sure what Mr. Thayer is driving at. I am actually quoting the witness, so let the witness give us an answer, both to Mr. Thayer's question and to my question. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Again, my problem, Mr. President, is he's not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: -- quoting the witness. He's building in premises into the questions, and if he wants to ask those questions, I've got no problem with that. If he wants to ask the first question: In addition to uniforms, did you have any information that the Ukrainians sold weapons to the Bosnians? I have no problem with that question. But building it in without any foundation, and when we have an answer to a compound question, that's part of the problem that we have here is we've got multiple premises being built into a question with no real foundation laid.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: To shorten this discussion, I would like to ask

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sir, do you have any information that the Bosnian Serbs got -- sorry, I mean Bosnian Muslims got any weapons from the Ukrainian soldiers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At that point, I didn't know anything about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: What do you mean by "at that point"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You asked whether I knew that at the time. All I can do is describe what I saw at the time which was that some wore camouflage gear, others were armed, but I didn't know at the time what the origin was of those arms. I still don't know, but they were, in my view, in my opinion, Ukrainian uniforms.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Have you now some knowledge about weapons gained from the Ukrainians?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't have any knowledge of that now either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You need your microphone.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I ask a leading question or can I ask a question about anything that I need to know and do not know. I fail to comprehend why I am being limited in asking my questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Again, Mr. President. This is not any effort to limit General Tolimir's questioning. I hope I have made that clear on this occasion and other occasions. The question is solely the proper way of asking the questions so that we don't have a record that is misleading that we can't make sense of at the end of the day, and that's the problem with compound questions and questions that incorporate premises that have no foundation. So there is no limitation as far as the Prosecution is concerned with these questions, they just need to be asked in a proper way. That is all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Indeed, compound questions are always a problem as we have seen earlier today. You have heard the position of the Prosecution, Mr. Tolimir. Just put the next question to the witness. Carry on, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Presiding Judge. This is a Colonel who is able to give us an answer to these questions, so I should like to repeat.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: You say they bought the uniforms from some Ukrainians in Zepa. This is what you say, line 20. Mr. Thayer has expressed doubts about the use of the word "bought." Is this a fact?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: No, this is a misunderstanding. Please put just your next question. It's much better than to repeat some concerns again. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Did the Muslims buy their uniforms from the Ukrainians, to the best of your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS
utterances.text: I saw that they were wearing them. I was not present at the time of purchase, of course. But because they were wearing Ukrainian uniforms, it could have originated from them, but I don't know that. Some Muslims were wearing such a uniform and I did make a statement about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you observe any insignia that told you that those uniforms were, indeed, Ukrainian?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS
utterances.text: I can't remember that anymore.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I will not belabour this point. In your statement on page 2, paragraph 3, lines 1 to 5, I will quote: "The next day, Sunday, 9 July 1995, two British SAS units arrived. They requested a Netherlands forward air control. Sergeant Bosch and his crew drove to the southern part of the enclave to find out where the Bosnian Serbs were. Later, the group was replaced by the quick reaction force of the Charlie Company. An hour after Bosch had left, he told us over the radio that he had been surrounded by Bosnian Serbian soldiers at the Swedish shelter, that they had been disarmed and were being taken to Bratunac." My question: Had these soldiers gone to Srebrenica before this or were they just there the next day when, as you say, on Sunday, the 9th of July, the British SAS arrived?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS
utterances.text: Could you perhaps phrase the question more clearly because I can't understand whether you are asking about the British or the Dutch?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I am asking about the British unit because you say, "The next day on Sunday, 9 July, two British SAS arrived." I am asking about them. Was it that they arrived on Srebrenica only on the 9th of July, the Brits?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS
utterances.text: In this statement, I describe that I was at blocking position 1 but that on Sunday, 9 July, two British SASers arrived, so they had been in the enclave before that, but that day they arrived at blocking position 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know whether these soldiers were part of the UNPROFOR or were they a distinct SAS unit outside the UNPROFOR structure?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS
utterances.text: These soldiers were assigned to our special forces and had been -- had already been in the enclave for quite some time under UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Was the SAS subordinated to the commander of the Dutch battalion in view of the fact that you say they requested a Netherlands forward air control?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS
utterances.text: They worked with our special forces and were under our authority, so I assume that that's what your question concerns.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Were they part of the UNPROFOR quota or contingent and that of the Dutch battalion or were they separate, were they outside that structure because you say they requested a Netherlands forward air control?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS
utterances.text: Based on their expertise they thought that it was a good place from blocking position 1 where we had a clear view of the south of the enclave to deploy any forward air controllers. So they were being accommodated on our compound and worked with our special forces, and they arrived on sight and said that it would be a good idea to deploy a Dutch forward air controller here. I agreed with them, and that's what I requested.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. The SAS unit, did they report to your commander or to somebody else within or outside the enclave?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS
utterances.text: I don't know that clearly, but they were not part of my platoon at that point. They were part of the special forces, and they arranged how the reporting would proceed. But if you mean something more specific, I will try to help you with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did they receive orders from Karremans or from somebody else? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS
utterances.text: I don't know exactly. At that point in the enclave they had multiple communication devices, but I can't help you with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. You said in the third paragraph, second line: "Sergeant Bosch and his crew drove to the southern part of the enclave to find out where the Bosnian Serbs were. Later, the group was replaced by the quick reaction force of the Charlie Company. An hour after Bosch had left, he told us over the radio that he had been surrounded by Bosnian Serbian soldiers at the Swedish shelter, that they had been disarmed and were being taken to Bratunac." Have I quoted you faithfully? And if I have, tell me why did he go to find out where the Bosnian Serbs were and why did he immediately request for a Dutch forward air control?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS
utterances.text: I am going to have to explain this to you. Blocking position Bravo 1 were APCs and that blocking position was a good location to put forward air controllers in position because they had a good view of the south of the enclave from there. That's how it reads. And after that, it says that Sergeant Bosch went with his crew to the south of the enclave. This was simply an infantry group in an armoured vehicle. And that was in the south of the enclave, the Swedish shelter, and he had instructions to investigate whether the Bosnian Serbs had already penetrated the enclave in the south, and what you can infer is that one hour after he drove from my position with his infantry group to the south, he was surrounded by Bosnian Serbs and disarmed. That's separate from the forward air controllers.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: You use the sentence "to find the Bosnian Serbs." Can you tell us where the Bosnian Serbs were then and where the Muslims were then relative to you and relative to Sergeant Bosch?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS
utterances.text: At that point I was in blocking position 1. We had no view of the activities of the Bosnian Serbs in the south. Ordinarily, the Swedish shelter would have accommodated Muslims. He was supposed to go there, and the moment he arrived there he was surrounded by Bosnian Serbs. We might infer from that that the Bosnian Serbs had penetrated the enclave in the area of the Swedish shelter, surrounded Sergeant Bosch there and disarmed him and transported him off to Bratunac. The Muslims were concentrated more in the north, some of them near my blocking position.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. How far was that from Bosch and from the Swedish shelter? How far back was that? What was the distance between that place and the Muslim positions in the centre of the enclave in kilometres?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS
utterances.text: I would have to check on a map, but I estimate about 2 kilometres as the crow flies.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: In front of you, between you and the Swedish shelter there were no Muslims. Why did Sergeant Bosch look for the Serbs then? Why did he venture among the Serbs knowing there were no Muslims there, there was nobody to protect them -- protect him there? Is it possible that he wanted to protect the area although there were no Muslims there?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS
utterances.text: His instructions were to determine whether Bosnian Serbs had already penetrated the enclave, and he did find that out because he was surrounded and disarmed. But we had no perception, no observation in the south of the enclave because our observation posts were fired at and toppled.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Can we then say that Sergeant Bosch entered the Swedish shelter which had already been in the hands of the Army of Republika Srpska by then?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS
utterances.text: I don't know. All I know is that the sergeant travelled to the south from my blocking position and made this announcement over the radio to me. I don't know exactly what it was like on site there, whether Bosnian Serb troops were already in the Swedish shelter or whether they were en route.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I asked you because you say, in your statement, and I quote: "In the Swedish shelter, he was surrounded by Bosnian Serbs, they disarmed him and took him to Bratunac. There was no fighting. He was just disarmed there." Let me ask you, was there any fighting there or not? And based on your answer we will try and conclude whether he had fallen into a trap which was the Swedish shelter in the possession of the Serbs, or whether he was disarmed after some fighting.

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS
utterances.text: I don't know whether he was involved in fighting. He reported to me that he was surrounded and disarmed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you for your answer. A while ago, you said that you were not sure whether they got their orders from Karremans or from somebody else. Based on your answer, I would like to ask you this: Was he perhaps disarmed because the Serbs knew that he was not a member of the DutchBat but, rather, that he was a member of the SAS, the special forces of the great British army? Thank you?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS
utterances.text: I think I have explained clearly what the situation was like. Sergeant Bosch was a Dutch sergeant who, with his Dutch infantry group, drove to the south. There were only two British in the enclave and they stayed with me in the blocking position. So in the south, only Dutch UNPROFOR soldiers in Dutch attire in a Dutch armoured vehicle were present. The two British remained at Bravo 1. Sergeant Bosch is a Dutchman.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you for your explanation. Thank you for telling us that Sergeant Bosch was a Dutchman. Did he receive his orders from the SAS to go to that place where he was then surrounded by the Serbian army troops?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS
utterances.text: The two British military in the enclave had a lower rank and were accommodated with our special forces. They had no influence whatsoever on Dutch UNPROFOR troops. They did not command anybody. Sergeant Bosch was instructed by Captain Groen to drive to the south. The two British are entirely outside of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Again, thank you for your explanation. You say page 2, paragraph 4, lines 2 and 3: "On several occasions I saw a tank approaching them from the south." Whose tank was that and who was the tank approaching? It is not very clear from your statement, could you please explain.

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS
utterances.text: In the statement, I state that I saw a Bosnian Serb tank entering the enclave, firing a number of times, and then leaving again. It was a Serb tank 54/55.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I am reading from your statement. I am quoting you, and additionally you said: "I didn't see what part had been hit, but I saw smoke." My question is this: That tank that you had previously seen or that you saw at the time, was that tank hit and was smoke coming from the tank?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS
utterances.text: The Bosnian Serb tank entering the enclave fired at the city of Srebrenica as well as at villagers in the surroundings. The tank was not hit. The tank caused the smoke. I couldn't see exactly which house was hit. I did see smoke rising up.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Again, thank you for your explanation. Did you have the authority to fire upon the tank because that tank had previously opened fire on a sector, on a facility, or a military target that you, yourself, did not observe or see? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS
utterances.text: Are you asking whether I was allowed to open fire at the Serb tank?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I am asking you: Were you authorised to open fire if you didn't know whether it was targeting a firing position or if it had hit a sector or an empty facility or a target that was unknown to you; in other words, you didn't know what the target was?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS
utterances.text: At that point I knew that the firing was not at us, UNPROFOR, but a Serbian village or at the city of Srebrenica, and that's what I reported to my commander, Captain Groen. And he kept asking me, Is there firing at us or somebody else? And if they were firing at us, I would have been authorised to return fire, but I did not have equipment, weapons, to fire at a tank. All I had was a weapon with a range of 800 metres. So regarding your question as to whether I was authorised to open fire independently on a Serb tank, the answer is no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Just while we are here to save a little bit of time later on, there is a reference in the transcript to page 75, line 15, to a Serbian village. The answer is: "At that point I knew that the firing was not at us, UNPROFOR, but a Serbian village or at the city of Srebrenica, and that's what I reported to my commander." I expect that there is an error somewhere in that. I won't say much more than that, but just to save some redistrict, I guess, if we can deal with it now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir could you clarify --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Maybe it would be best.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I state that I did indeed not say that, that I said a Bosnian village, such as Pusmulici.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. That clarifies the situation, in my view. Mr. Tolimir, now is your last question for today. If you are looking at this clock here in the courtroom, it is wrong. We are approaching 7.00 already. But you have still time for a last question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: And my last question is on page 2 where you say in the last paragraph, in the last two lines of that paragraph, page 2, paragraph 4, lines 10 and 11 where you say: "At one point fire was opened at us, either from a tank or artillery weapons from south-east. Fire was opened five times. It is possible that Serbs opened fire on Muslims. They were 5 to 10 metres away from us."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I don't find this relevant portion in the transcript. Could you check that, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: We just need to go to the next page, Mr. President, at the very top. That's the portion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it's on page 3 in the English version, and my question is as follows.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Was the distance of 5 metres from you visible for that tank, and that was where the Muslims were, according to you. And could the firing positions be discernible from the tank if that's where you were and if that's where the Muslims were?

utterances.speaker: VINCENTIUS EGBERS
utterances.text: At blocking position 1, a artillery device of the Muslims was indeed positioned. I asked the commander -- I requested the commander not to fire with that piece of artillery because we were very close by, perhaps 50 to 60 metres from there. They jotted that down on a slip of paper and reported that to their commander and since then that piece of artillery was not used. When we were under fire, I could not say with absolute certainty to my commander that the fire was directed at UNPROFOR. It could also have been directed at the Muslims that had a piece of artillery there. That was the situation. When we were fired at, we moved to a different position. Only later on when that position came under fire as well did I tell my commander that the fire was directed at us. The grenades that hit, in the passage of text you are referring to, they fell right near us and resulted in a minor injury.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much for your answer. It is two minutes past 7.00 already and therefore we have to adjourn for today, and we will assume tomorrow in the afternoon in this courtroom, 2.15. May I remind you that it is not allowed during the break to have contact with either party about the content of your testimony. Thank you very much. We adjourn.
